focus: Exodus 15 turns the deliverance at the sea into worship, as Moses and Israel sing of the LORD who has triumphed over Pharaoh and will bring His redeemed people to His holy dwelling, and Miriam leads the women in reply. The chapter then begins the journey from the sea, where bitter water at Marah becomes a test and the LORD reveals Himself as the One who heals His people.

sections.title: The LORD Has Triumphed over Pharaoh at the Sea
sections.summary: Moses and Israel sing, “I will sing to the LORD, For He has triumphed gloriously!” (Exodus 15:1), praising Him as their strength, song, and salvation. The song celebrates how the LORD’s right hand shattered the enemy, how the waters stood up at the blast of His nostrils, and how Pharaoh’s army sank like lead when He blew with His wind.

sections.title: The Incomparable LORD Leads His Redeemed to His Dwelling
sections.summary: The song asks, “Who is like You, O LORD, among the gods?” (Exodus 15:11), and declares that He has led His redeemed people in mercy to His holy habitation while the nations tremble. He will plant them in the place He has made for His own dwelling, and the song ends, “The LORD shall reign forever and ever” (Exodus 15:18).

sections.title: Miriam Leads the Women in Answering Song
sections.summary: The narrator recalls that Pharaoh’s horses and chariots went into the sea while Israel walked on dry land. Miriam the prophetess takes a timbrel, the women follow her with timbrels and dances, and she answers with the song’s opening words.

sections.title: The LORD Heals the Bitter Water at Marah and Brings Israel to Elim
sections.summary: After three days without water, Israel finds only bitter water at Marah and complains, and the LORD shows Moses a tree that makes the water sweet. There He tests them, promises to put none of Egypt’s diseases on them if they heed His voice, for “I am the LORD who heals you” (Exodus 15:26), and then brings them to Elim with its twelve wells and seventy palm trees.

1.brief: Moses and the children of Israel sing to the LORD, “I will sing to the LORD, For He has triumphed gloriously! The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea!” Israel’s first response on the far shore is worship that gives all the credit to God.
1.explain:
“Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the LORD, and spoke, saying:”

Israel’s first response on the far shore is song. Moses leads, and the whole people join. The song is sung “to the LORD,” addressed to Him and in His honor. This is the first song recorded in the Bible.

“I will sing to the LORD, For He has triumphed gloriously!”

The singer gives the reason for singing. The word translated triumphed gloriously reads literally He is highly exalted or He has risen up gloriously. God has shown Himself supreme.

“The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea!”

The opening verse sums up what happened. “He has thrown” Egypt’s chariot force “into the sea.” The song gives all the credit to God. Israel did not fight. The LORD won the battle. Revelation 15:3 later pictures the redeemed singing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb,” joining this deliverance at the sea to God’s final victory over His enemies.

2.brief: “The LORD is my strength and song, And He has become my salvation,” and the singers promise to praise and exalt Him as their God and their fathers’ God. The LORD is not only the One who saved them but the One they now sing about.
2.explain:
“The LORD is my strength and song, And He has become my salvation;”

The singer moves from what God did to who He is. “The LORD is my strength,” the source of power. He is also the singer’s “song,” the theme of praise. He “has become my salvation.” The word salvation echoes Moses’ promise at the sea, “see the salvation of the LORD” (14:13). What God promised, He has now done.

“He is my God, and I will praise Him; My father’s God, and I will exalt Him.”

The singer claims God personally, “my God,” and also as “My father’s God,” the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The God who made promises to the fathers has kept them. The singer responds by praising and exalting Him.
2.notes: The words of the first line appear again in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2. Later generations used the song of the sea to praise God for new deliverances.

3.brief: “The LORD is a man of war; The LORD is His name.” The song celebrates the LORD as the warrior who fought for His people, as Moses promised in Exodus 14:14.
3.explain:
“The LORD is a man of war;”

The song calls the LORD “a man of war,” a warrior. Moses had promised, “The LORD will fight for you” (14:14). He did, and Israel now praises Him as the one who fought.

“The LORD is His name.”

This is the name God revealed to Moses (3:14–15; 6:2–3). Through the battle at the sea, He has shown what His name means.

4.brief: Pharaoh’s chariots and army He has cast into the sea, and his chosen captains are drowned in the Red Sea. The song recalls Egypt’s mighty army brought to nothing.
4.explain:
“Pharaoh’s chariots and his army He has cast into the sea;”

The song recalls the defeat. God “cast” Pharaoh’s chariots and army into the sea, like a man throwing something away.

“His chosen captains also are drowned in the Red Sea.”

Even Egypt’s “chosen captains,” the elite officers (14:7), were “drowned.” Egypt’s best fighters were helpless before the LORD.

5.brief: The depths have covered them, and they sank to the bottom like a stone. The picture of a stone sinking shows how swiftly and completely Egypt’s army was lost.
5.explain:
“The depths have covered them; They sank to the bottom like a stone.”

“The depths” closed over the army. They went down quickly, with no chance of rising. The picture of a stone shows how swiftly and completely Egypt’s army was lost.

6.brief: “Your right hand, O LORD, has become glorious in power,” and the same hand has shattered the enemy. The song turns to address the LORD directly and praises His power.
6.explain:
“Your right hand, O LORD, has become glorious in power;”

The song now speaks to God directly. The “right hand” was the hand of strength and skill. God’s “right hand” has shown itself “glorious in power.”

“Your right hand, O LORD, has dashed the enemy in pieces.”

The line repeats “Your right hand, O LORD” for emphasis, then completes the thought. God has “dashed the enemy in pieces,” shattered them. Repetition is a mark of Hebrew poetry.

7.brief: In the greatness of His excellence the LORD overthrew those who rose against Him and sent His wrath, which consumed them like stubble. Those who opposed Israel are described as rising against God Himself.
7.explain:
“And in the greatness of Your excellence You have overthrown those who rose against You;”

God’s “excellence,” His majesty, is shown in His victory. Egypt’s army is described as “those who rose against You.” By attacking Israel, Egypt set itself against God. Those who opposed Israel are described as rising against God Himself.

“You sent forth Your wrath; It consumed them like stubble.”

God’s “wrath” went out like fire and “consumed them like stubble,” dry straw that burns up instantly. The enemy had no more strength against God than straw against fire.

8.brief: At the blast of the LORD’s nostrils the waters were gathered and the floods stood upright like a heap. The song pictures the dividing of the sea as the breath of God holding back the waters.
8.explain:
“And with the blast of Your nostrils The waters were gathered together;”

The song describes the east wind (14:21) as “the blast of Your nostrils,” God’s breath. At His breath “the waters were gathered together.”

“The floods stood upright like a heap; The depths congealed in the heart of the sea.”

The water “stood upright like a heap.” The deep waters “congealed,” became firm, in the middle of the sea. The poetry matches the narrative’s picture of the waters as a wall (14:22). The song pictures the dividing of the sea as the breath of God holding back the waters.

9.brief: The song gives the enemy’s boast: “I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil,” with his promise to draw his sword and destroy them. The enemy’s confident plans set up their sudden reversal in the next verse.
9.explain:
“The enemy said, ‘I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil;”

The song quotes the enemy’s boast. He speaks again and again of what he will do. He boasts that he will “pursue,” “overtake,” and “divide the spoil,” sharing out the plunder.

“My desire shall be satisfied on them. I will draw my sword, My hand shall destroy them.”

He expects to have his fill of vengeance. He will “draw my sword,” and “My hand shall destroy them.” The enemy trusted his own hand. Set beside God’s right hand (15:6), his hand amounts to nothing. The enemy’s confident plans set up their sudden reversal in the next verse.

10.brief: The LORD blew with His wind, the sea covered them, and they sank like lead in the mighty waters. One breath from God undid all the enemy’s boasts.
10.explain:
“You blew with Your wind, The sea covered them;”

One line answers the enemy’s six boasts. “You blew with Your wind,” and the sea covered them. One breath from God undid all the enemy’s plans.

“They sank like lead in the mighty waters.”

They “sank like lead,” heavy and helpless, in “the mighty waters.”

11.brief: “Who is like You, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like You, glorious in holiness, Fearful in praises, doing wonders?” The song declares that no god can compare with the LORD in holiness and power.
11.explain:
“Who is like You, O LORD, among the gods?”

The song asks a question with only one answer. Egypt had many gods, and none could save it (12:12). No god compares with the LORD.

“Who is like You, glorious in holiness, Fearful in praises, doing wonders?”

The LORD is “glorious in holiness,” utterly pure and set apart. He is “fearful in praises,” worthy of awe even as He is praised. He is the God “doing wonders.” The song declares that no god can compare with the LORD in holiness and power.
11.notes: The question “Who is like You?” echoes through Israel’s worship (Psalm 35:10; 71:19; 89:6–8; Micah 7:18). The name Michael means Who is like God?

12.brief: The LORD stretched out His right hand, and the earth swallowed the enemy. The song again credits the victory to God’s own hand.
12.explain:
“You stretched out Your right hand; The earth swallowed them.”

God “stretched out Your right hand,” and “the earth swallowed them.” The word “earth” here may refer to the sea floor or more broadly to the underworld, the place of the dead. The song again credits the victory to God’s own hand.

13.brief: “You in Your mercy have led forth The people whom You have redeemed,” guiding them in strength to His holy habitation. The song turns from judgment to the LORD’s faithful love in leading His redeemed people toward His dwelling.
13.explain:
“You in Your mercy have led forth The people whom You have redeemed;”

The song turns from judgment to love. God led His people “in Your mercy,” His steadfast covenant love. They are “the people whom You have redeemed,” bought back from slavery. God had promised, “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm” (6:6).

“You have guided them in Your strength To Your holy habitation.”

God has “guided them” toward “Your holy habitation,” the place where He dwells. The song speaks of the journey as already done, so sure is the outcome. God is leading His redeemed people toward His dwelling.
13.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “mercy” is chesed, God’s loyal, steadfast love to His covenant people.

The “holy habitation” may refer to Sinai, to the promised land, or to the place where God would later set His sanctuary. The song looks toward all of these as God brings His people to Himself (15:17).

14.brief: The peoples will hear and be afraid, and sorrow will grip the inhabitants of Philistia. News of the LORD’s victory will spread to the nations along Israel’s way.
14.explain:
“The people will hear and be afraid;”

The song looks ahead. “The people” of the nations “will hear” of what God did at the sea and “be afraid.”

“Sorrow will take hold of the inhabitants of Philistia.”

The first nation named is “Philistia,” along the coast road God avoided (13:17). “Sorrow,” writhing like a woman in labor, will grip them.

15.brief: The chiefs of Edom will be dismayed, trembling will seize the mighty men of Moab, and all the inhabitants of Canaan will melt away. The song looks ahead to the nations Israel will meet on the way to the land.
15.explain:
“Then the chiefs of Edom will be dismayed;”

“The chiefs of Edom,” descendants of Esau south of the Dead Sea, will be terrified.

“The mighty men of Moab, Trembling will take hold of them;”

“The mighty men of Moab,” east of the Dead Sea, will tremble.

“All the inhabitants of Canaan will melt away.”

The people of Canaan will lose their courage. The song looks ahead to the nations Israel will meet on the way to the land.
15.notes: Rahab later told the spies in Jericho, “we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea for you,” and “all the inhabitants of the land are fainthearted because of you” (Joshua 2:9–10). The song’s expectation was fulfilled.

16.brief: Fear and dread will fall on them, making them still as a stone “Till Your people pass over, O LORD.” The LORD will hold back the nations until the people He has purchased pass through.
16.explain:
“Fear and dread will fall on them;”

“Fear and dread” will grip the nations.

“By the greatness of Your arm They will be as still as a stone,”

By God’s power they will be “as still as a stone.” The Egyptians sank like a stone (15:5). The nations will freeze like a stone, unable to act against Israel.

“Till Your people pass over, O LORD, Till the people pass over Whom You have purchased.”

They will stand still “till Your people pass over.” Israel will pass through or across into the land. The people are those “whom You have purchased,” acquired as God’s own possession. The LORD will hold back the nations until the people He has purchased pass through.
16.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “purchased” can mean to acquire or to create. The same verb is used in Deuteronomy 32:6, “Is He not your Father, who bought you?”

17.brief: The LORD will bring His people in and plant them in the mountain of His inheritance, in the place He has made “For Your own dwelling.” The goal of the exodus is God’s people dwelling with Him in the place He has prepared.
17.explain:
“You will bring them in and plant them In the mountain of Your inheritance,”

God will “bring them in and plant them,” like a gardener planting a tree to stay. The place is “the mountain of Your inheritance,” the mountain God claims as His own possession.

“In the place, O LORD, which You have made For Your own dwelling,”

The song names this place as the one God has made “For Your own dwelling.” God will plant His people in the land He promised, and there He will have a place where He dwells among them.

“The sanctuary, O Lord, which Your hands have established.”

The song names the place “The sanctuary,” a holy place “which Your hands have established.” That chosen dwelling later found its expression at Mount Zion, where the temple stood (Psalm 78:54, 68–69). The goal of the exodus is God’s people dwelling with Him in the place He has prepared.
17.notes: The song looks toward the place God would choose for His name (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11).

18.brief: “The LORD shall reign forever and ever.” The song ends by declaring the LORD’s everlasting kingship.
18.explain:
“The LORD shall reign forever and ever.”

The song ends by declaring God’s kingship. Pharaoh had claimed authority over Israel. Now the LORD is shown to be King, and His reign has no end. “Forever and ever.” The song ends by declaring the LORD’s everlasting kingship.
18.notes: This is the first time Scripture speaks of the LORD reigning as King.

19.brief: The narrator recalls that Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen went into the sea and the LORD brought the waters back on them, while Israel went on dry land. The summary ties the song back to the events of the crossing.
19.explain:
“For the horses of Pharaoh went with his chariots and his horsemen into the sea,”

The narrator steps back and summarizes the event behind the song. Pharaoh’s whole force went “into the sea.”

“and the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them.”

The narrator again names God as the one who acted.

“But the children of Israel went on dry land in the midst of the sea.”

Israel went through on “dry land.” The summary ties the song back to the events of the crossing.

20.brief: Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, takes a timbrel, and all the women follow her with timbrels and dances. The women join in the celebration, led by Miriam.
20.explain:
“Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron,”

“Miriam” is called “the prophetess,” the first woman given that title in Scripture. She is named as “the sister of Aaron” and was also Moses’ sister (Numbers 26:59). She is likely the sister who watched over the infant Moses at the Nile (2:4, 7).

“took the timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.”

Miriam takes “the timbrel,” a small hand drum like a tambourine. “All the women” follow with timbrels and dancing. The women join in the celebration, led by Miriam.
20.notes: Micah 6:4 names Miriam with Moses and Aaron as leaders God sent before Israel.

21.brief: Miriam answers them, “Sing to the LORD, For He has triumphed gloriously!” repeating the song’s opening words. Her song gives the whole community a voice in praising God.
21.explain:
“And Miriam answered them:”

Miriam “answered them,” responding in song, perhaps in a call-and-response with the singers.

“Sing to the LORD, For He has triumphed gloriously! The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea!”

Miriam’s song repeats the opening of Moses’ song (15:1). Moses said “I will sing.” Miriam calls everyone to “Sing to the LORD.” Her song gives the whole community a voice in praising God.

22.brief: Moses brings Israel from the Red Sea into the Wilderness of Shur, and after three days they find no water. The journey toward Sinai begins with a hard test right after the great victory.
22.explain:
“So Moses brought Israel from the Red Sea; then they went out into the Wilderness of Shur.”

The journey continues. Moses leads Israel from the sea into “the Wilderness of Shur,” the dry region east of Egypt.

“And they went three days in the wilderness and found no water.”

After “three days” they have “found no water.” In the desert this was a crisis. The journey toward Sinai begins with a hard test right after the great victory.
22.notes: Shur means wall. The wilderness of Shur lay in the northwestern Sinai Peninsula. Hagar fled toward Shur (Genesis 16:7).

23.brief: At Marah they cannot drink the water because it is bitter, so the place is called Marah. The name records the bitterness of the disappointment.
23.explain:
“Now when they came to Marah, they could not drink the waters of Marah, for they were bitter.”

At last they find water at “Marah,” but it is “bitter,” undrinkable. Their hope turns to disappointment.

“Therefore the name of it was called Marah.”

The place is named for its water. “Marah” means bitter. The name records the bitterness of the disappointment.
23.notes: Naomi later says, “Call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me” (Ruth 1:20). The name is from the same root.

24.brief: The people complain against Moses, saying, “What shall we drink?” Their song turns quickly to grumbling when need arises.
24.explain:
“And the people complained against Moses, saying, ‘What shall we drink?”

Three days after singing God’s praise, the people “complained against Moses.” To complain means to grumble or murmur. Their song turns quickly to grumbling when need arises. This is the first of many complaints in the wilderness (16:2; 17:3; Numbers 11:1; 14:2).

25.brief: Moses cries out to the LORD, who shows him a tree, and when Moses casts it into the water, the water becomes sweet; there God makes a statute for them and tests them. God meets the need and uses it to test His people.
25.explain:
“So he cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a tree.”

Moses does what the people did not. He “cried out to the LORD.” God answers by showing him “a tree,” a piece of wood.

“When he cast it into the waters, the waters were made sweet.”

Moses throws it into the water, and “the waters were made sweet.” The text does not say the wood had any natural power to sweeten water. God made the water drinkable when Moses obeyed.

“There He made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there He tested them,”

At Marah God “made a statute and an ordinance,” a standing rule for Israel. He also “tested them.” God meets the need and uses it to test His people. The test is whether they will trust and listen to Him.
25.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “showed” is related to the word torah, meaning instruction. God taught Moses what to do.

26.brief: God promises that if they diligently heed His voice and keep His commands, He will put none of Egypt’s diseases on them, “For I am the LORD who heals you.” The LORD reveals Himself as Israel’s healer and links His promise to their obedience.
26.explain:
“and said, ‘If you diligently heed the voice of the LORD your God and do what is right in His sight,”

God gives the terms of His promise. Israel is to “diligently heed the voice of the LORD,” listening carefully, and to “do what is right in His sight.”

“give ear to His commandments and keep all His statutes,”

They are to listen to and keep His “commandments” and “statutes.” The call to obey comes before Sinai and prepares Israel for the covenant there.

“I will put none of the diseases on you which I have brought on the Egyptians.”

The promise looks back to Egypt. God had brought plagues and “diseases” on the Egyptians, such as the boils (9:8–11). If Israel listens to Him, He will not bring such diseases on them.

“For I am the LORD who heals you.”

God reveals Himself by a new title: “the LORD who heals you.” He healed the bitter water, and He is the healer of His people. The LORD reveals Himself as Israel’s healer and links His promise to their obedience.
26.notes: The Hebrew phrase is often transliterated “Yahweh Rapha.” The verb means to heal or restore. Psalm 103:3 praises the LORD “who heals all your diseases.” Deuteronomy 28:27, 60 warns that disobedience would bring the diseases of Egypt on Israel.

27.brief: Israel comes to Elim, where there are twelve wells and seventy palm trees, and they camp by the waters. After the test at Marah, God brings His people to a place of refreshment.
27.explain:
“Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve wells of water and seventy palm trees;”

After Marah comes “Elim,” an oasis with “twelve wells” and “seventy palm trees.” After the test, God brings His people to plenty.

“so they camped there by the waters.”

Israel camps “by the waters.” After the test at Marah, God brings His people to a place of refreshment.
27.notes: Elim means large trees or terebinths. It is often identified with Wadi Gharandel on the western side of the Sinai Peninsula, though the location is uncertain.
